title: Personal Information
goals: Meet new neighbors and talk about yourself: where you are from, what you do and where you live.

learn.title: Simple Present and Present Continuous (review)
learn.html:
Use the Simple Present for habits, routines and facts. Use the Present Continuous for actions happening now or around now.

Simple PresentPresent Continuous
Usehabits, facts, permanent situationsnow, temporary situations
PositiveShe works in a bank.She is working at home today.
NegativeHe doesn't live here.He isn't living here this month.
QuestionDo you work on Saturdays?Are you working now?
Time wordsalways, usually, every day, often, nevernow, right now, today, this week, at the moment
  • Add -s with he / she / it in the Simple Present: she lives.
  • Some verbs are not usually used in the continuous: know, like, love, want, need, have (for possession).

watch.wrong: She is work in a hospital.
watch.why: For a regular job, use the Simple Present. The continuous needs is + verb-ing.
Know is a state verb. We do not use it in the continuous.
With he / she / it, use doesn't.
Questions in the Simple Present need do / does.

learn.title: Simple Past and used to
learn.html:
Use the Simple Past for finished actions at a specific time in the past. Use used to for past habits or situations that are not true now.

Simple Pastused to
PositiveWe moved here in 2019.I used to live in a small town.
NegativeShe didn't speak English.We didn't use to have a car.
QuestionDid you grow up here?Did you use to play soccer?
  • Regular verbs end in -ed: move - moved. Irregular verbs change: go - went, meet - met, have - had.
  • After did / didn't, the verb goes back to the base form: Did you go?
  • used to + base verb. It does not tell us exactly when something happened.

watch.why: After didn't, use the base form.

watch.wrong: I use to live in Toluca.
watch.right: I used to live in Toluca.
watch.why: For the past, write used to, with -d.
After did, the verb is in the base form.

watch.wrong: I used to living with my parents.
watch.right: I used to live with my parents.

learn.title: Future: will and be going to
learn.html:
We use be going to for plans we already made and for predictions based on what we see. We use will for quick decisions, promises, offers and opinions about the future.

UseExample
plan (be going to)We are going to visit my aunt next month.
prediction with evidence (be going to)Look at the sky! It is going to rain.
quick decision (will)The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.
promise or offer (will)Don't worry. I'll help you with the boxes.
opinion (will)I think you'll like this neighborhood.
  • will + base verb for all subjects: she will go. Negative: won't.
  • be going to + base verb: I am going to study.

watch.wrong: She will to call you tomorrow.
watch.why: After will, use the base verb without to.

watch.wrong: He will goes to the party.
watch.right: He will go to the party.

watch.wrong: They are going to moving next month.
watch.right: They are going to move next month.
I am going to study tonight.
watch.why: Do not forget the verb be: am / is / are.

learn.title: Meeting neighbors and asking for help
learn.html:
• Hi, I'm... I just moved into number 5. - introducing yourself to a neighbor.
  • Welcome to the neighborhood! - welcoming a new neighbor.
  • Nice to meet you. Where are you from? - starting a friendly conversation.
  • What do you do? / What do you do for a living? - asking about someone's job.
  • I'm new here. Could you help me? - asking for help when you arrive.
  • Could you tell me where the nearest pharmacy is? - a polite question (the verb is after the subject).
  • Do you know how to get to the bus station? - asking for directions.
  • Where can I find...? / Is there a... near here? - looking for places and services.
  • Thanks a lot. I really appreciate it. - thanking someone for help.

write.model:
My name is Daniel Torres, and I'm 29 years old. I was born in Puebla, Mexico, but I live in Querétaro now. I moved here in 2021 because I got a job as a software tester. Before that, I used to live with my parents and my two sisters. I grew up in a small neighborhood where everybody knew each other, so at first I felt homesick. Now I'm used to my new city, and I have many good friends.

I work from Monday to Friday, and I usually play soccer on Saturday mornings. This semester I'm studying English at night because I want to improve my career. In the future, I'm going to take an online course in data analysis. I think I will also travel to Canada one day. I love meeting new people, learning languages and trying different food.

reading.title: New Country, New Life
reading.intro: Read about three people who moved to a new country and answer.
paragraphs: Moving to a new country is never easy, but many people turn the change into a success story. Here are the stories of three people who started a new life far from home.

Karina Lopez grew up in Guadalajara, Mexico. In 2015, she moved to Canada to study design. At first she felt homesick, and she didn't understand fast English. She used to eat lunch alone every day. Then she joined a volunteer group in her neighborhood and made her first friends. Today she is a graphic designer, and she works for a large company in Vancouver. She is also learning French, and next year she is going to open her own studio.

Omar Haddad is from Egypt. He came to Spain in 2012 with only one suitcase. He didn't speak Spanish, so he took free classes at a community center every evening. He used to wash dishes in a restaurant; now he owns two small restaurants. "Be patient," he says. "Every day gets a little easier." This year he is hiring more workers from his neighborhood.

Mei Lin grew up in a small village in China. Five years ago, she moved to Australia to join her brother. She is a nurse now, and she is studying for an exam so she can work in a bigger hospital. She says her neighbors helped her a lot: they showed her the bus routes and invited her to dinner. "In the future, I'll do the same for other newcomers," she says.

These people have different backgrounds, but they share three things. They asked for help, they learned the language, and they never stopped trying. Their stories show that the first months are the hardest, but things get better. Karina, Omar and Mei Lin all say the same thing: be kind to yourself, make friends with your neighbors, and don't be afraid of mistakes. What will you do if you move to a new place?
